value.overview: The Sooty-capped Chlorospingus (Chlorospingus pileatus), also called the Sooty-capped Bush Tanager, is a small New World sparrow of the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is most closely associated with cool montane forests and dense vegetation. Often active and social, it searches for insects, other small arthropods, and fruit in the understory and middle levels of forest. Costa Rica contains most of the species’ global range and supports important populations on several mountain ranges and volcanoes.
value.classification: The species belongs to the family Passerellidae, the New World sparrows, and the genus Chlorospingus. It is not a true tanager, despite its former common name, Sooty-capped Bush Tanager.
value.identification: This compact bird has olive upperparts, a dark sooty or blackish crown and face, and a prominent white eyebrow stripe that extends back along the side of the head and neck. The throat is whitish and finely spotted, while the lower breast and belly are usually yellowish or pale, with olive-yellow coloring across the breast sides and flanks. Its bill is fairly thick. It resembles the Common Chlorospingus, but the Sooty-capped species has a longer, more conspicuous white supercilium rather than a small white spot behind the eye.
value.rangeHabitat: The Sooty-capped Chlorospingus occurs in Costa Rica and western Panama, with Costa Rica holding much of its restricted global distribution. In Costa Rica it is found mainly in the Cordillera de Tilarán and the Cordillera de Talamanca, including high volcanic and mountain areas such as the Cerro de la Muerte region. It inhabits montane evergreen forest, elfin forest, forest edges, mature secondary growth, dense shrubs, and mossy vegetation. It is generally encountered above about 2,000 meters in Costa Rica, although the species as a whole occupies elevations from roughly 1,500 to 3,000 meters.
value.migrationStatus: A year-round resident in Costa Rica and throughout its limited range. It does not undertake regular long-distance seasonal migration, although local movements may occur in response to food, weather, or elevation.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly from February through July. The nest is a bulky cup constructed from moss, liverworts, lichen, and other plant fibers. Nest sites may be placed in earthen banks, low shrubs, epiphytes, or sheltered mossy growth, sometimes several meters above the ground. Clutches generally contain one or two pale eggs marked with pinkish-brown speckles or blotches. Several adults have occasionally been associated with a nest, suggesting that cooperative breeding may occur, but details of incubation and parental care remain incompletely documented.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of small arthropods and fruit. It usually feeds from the understory to the middle levels of montane forest, searching dense shrubs, moss-covered branches, bromeliads, and clusters of dead leaves. During the breeding season it is often seen in pairs or small groups. At other times it may join larger groups and regularly participates in mixed-species feeding flocks. Wing and tail flicking are common while it forages.
value.behavior: The Sooty-capped Chlorospingus is active, social, and usually travels through dense vegetation in small, vocal groups. Outside the breeding season, groups may become considerably larger, sometimes including dozens of birds. It frequently joins mixed-species flocks in highland forests and often remains in the lower and middle vegetation layers. Its calls are high, thin, and lisping, while the song is a light, squeaky series of repeated notes. The species can be difficult to see despite its movement and frequent vocal activity.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is considered stable, with an estimated global population of at least 50,000 mature individuals.
